tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. schema.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.

content.text:
This is the Atira platform's spec for how a single run of your agent works, from local development through to a scored submission.

## What a run is
A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`. Your agent gets a task and logins for the challenge's websites. The run ends when the agent submits an answer or time runs out.

## Workflow
1. **Develop locally:** run `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` to get the scouting logins and the website URLs. It also points the hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your machine, with `local` as the key. Run `atira login` once and keep `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Nothing you do this way counts, and bids you enter on the tender portal don't count either.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package and starts a run in the same sandbox scored runs use. A test run can go up to 2 hours, but aim for under 20 minutes. The run page shows the full score breakdown, and `atira cancel` stops a run early.
3. **Scored submission:** each submission runs once on `public-1`, and that run is what the leaderboard ranks. The final ranking at the end of the hackathon uses a **private dataset**.

## Inside a run
- **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`. It returns:
  - `brief`: the task and its rules
  - `access`: each site's URL and credentials
  - `submission`: where the answer goes. For RFQ it's `site`, meaning you submit through the configurator website.
  - `answer_schema`
  - `expires_at`
  - LLM proxy info
- **Submit:**
  - A `400` with `issues` means the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, and you can fix it and send it again.
  - A `202` means the answer is final. The run ends, the token and logins stop working, and the agent has 10 seconds to exit.
  - On the site, validation messages appear in German.
- **User-Agent:** set your own. Python's default `Python-urllib/…` gets a 403.

## Sandbox and timing
- **Machine:** a Linux VM with a 1280×800 desktop and a headful Chromium already running, with the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) at `127.0.0.1:9222`.
- **Toolchains:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` directly), Python 3.12 with uv (no system pip), Rust, gcc, git, curl and jq.
- **Setup:** up to 5 minutes, untimed. It has network access but no credentials or secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run.
- **Model warm-up:** untimed. List the hosted models your agent uses in `agent.json` under `"models"`. The run waits for those to warm up, and `"models": []` skips the wait. An unknown model id rejects the package.
- **Run:** timed. **RFQ gets 20 minutes, and a run with no answer scores 0.**
- **Network:** the run is offline except for the platform API and the challenge sites, reached through `HTTP_PROXY` at `127.0.0.1:3128`.
- **Hosted-model outage:** if the platform's own hosted models are down for most of the run and the run ends without an answer, the run doesn't count. A scored run restarts once automatically.

## Browsers
- `agent.json` can ask for `"browsers": 1–4`. Browser *n* uses CDP port 9221+n and display `:n`.
- `CDP_URLS` lists all of them and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are.
- **Don't launch browsers of your own, headless ones included.** The platform stops them within seconds.
- Locally, `CDP_URLS` isn't set, so your agent starts its own browsers.

## LLM calls
- **Proxy:** every call goes through a metering proxy at `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>/...`, which forwards it unchanged.
- **Environment variables:** `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and the others are set in advance, so the providers' SDKs work without changes. The Gemini SDK is the exception: you have to set its base URL explicitly.
- **Hosted models:** free to use, but each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated prices.
- **Your own key:** your provider bills your key. Store it as a **team secret** (on the team page or through the API) rather than in the package, because packages are stored and a review agent reads them. A team can have at most 20 secrets, and names can't clash with platform variables.
- **Cost ranking:** cost uses the providers' published prices, and an upstream-reported cost takes precedence. A call that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price, and streamed calls count too. There's no spending limit, but the leaderboard ranks on cost.
- **Request size:** up to 32 MiB per request.
- **Development outside runs:** use your personal token in the header `x-atira-team-key`. You bring your own key, and this usage is never ranked.

## Key takeaways for your agent
- Finish and submit within **20 minutes**.
- Use the platform's browsers via `CDP_URLS` and don't start your own.
- Fill in `"models"` in `agent.json` so the run doesn't wait for every hosted model to warm up.
- Keep keys out of the package and store them as team secrets.
- Set a custom User-Agent.

# Atira starter kit

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's
browsers and shows how to call the free hosted models. Then it stops at `solve()` in `agent.py`, the place for your
agent. Out of the box it exits without an answer.

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

More browsers: set `"browsers": 2` (up to 4) in `agent.json`, then `await browsers.connect(playwright, 1)` attaches
to browser 2.

## The hosted models in short

Both are free and need no key of yours: runs get the variables, and locally `atira scout --env` sets them, pointed
at `atira models proxy`.

```python
import models

text = await models.ask_qwen("Which button submits this form? ...")          # QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
yes = await models.ask_clef({"page": page_text}, "Is this the current revision?")  # CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY
```

`models.qwen()` is an OpenAI SDK client, for tool calls, images and everything else. Clef is set only where the
platform hosts it; if your agent relies on it, list `"models": ["qwen", "clef"]` in `agent.json` so the run waits for
it to warm up. Another provider works with your own key through the run's metering proxy:
`$API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls`.

## Run it locally

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (open a new terminal after installing it, so
it is on your PATH) and the Atira CLI, signed in once with `atira login`.

Terminal 1: start the free models and leave it open.

The test run worked as expected, but it scored 0 because the agent exited after 3 seconds without submitting an answer. The run page is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/runs/run_c09adac095aa7529.

That's because this repo is still the unmodified Atira starter kit. The README says `solve()` in `agent.py` is an empty placeholder and "out of the box it exits without an answer". The sandbox side all worked:

- **Setup:** `uv sync` ran without errors.

lines: +# AGENTS.md — isar-labs · Atira EHL Challenge „From RFQ to bid"
+Dieses Dokument ist die verbindliche Arbeitsanweisung für alle Coding-Agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor) und Menschen
+im Team. Lies es vollständig, bevor du Code schreibst. Details stehen in `docs/` (Index unten); bei Widerspruch gilt
+die Reihenfolge: **Challenge-Brief der Plattform > dieses Dokument > docs/**.
+Wir bauen ein Agentensystem, das in einer Sandbox (20 min, bis zu 4 Chromium-Browser über CDP, nur Plattform +
+4 Websites erreichbar) ein öffentliches Tender beantwortet: Vergabeportal (Ausschreibung, Bieterfragen, Konfigurator),
+Lieferantenportal (Lastenheft/Spezifikation), ERP (Material, Bestand, Konditionen) und Webmail (Freigaben, TAN).
+Am Ende wird **ein** signiertes Angebot im Konfigurator des Vergabeportals abgegeben. Gewertet wird:
+**eligible (richtige Tender-Referenz) → Qualität 0–100 → Kosten × Zeit**. Gewinner: zuerst **privater Datensatz**
+(andere Websites, anderes Layout, andere Navigation, Informationen anders verteilt!), dann public, dann Eleganz.
+➡️ Wir optimieren für **Generalität und Korrektheit**, nicht für das öffentliche Szenario.
+## 2. Nicht verhandelbare Regeln (Fair Play — Verstoß = Disqualifikation)
+1. **Keine hardcodierten Szenario-Werte** in `agent/` — weder Code, Config, Prompts, Kommentare, Defaults, Fallbacks
+   noch Tests: keine Tender-Referenzen, Materialnummern, Preise, Rabatte, Keys (`VP-…`, `TZ-…`, `K-…`, `RP-…`, `PB-…`,
+   `MET-…`, `FX-…`, `ER-…`, `GR-…`), Logins, TANs, URLs-Pfade der Public-Sites. Werte aus dem **Brief** (den jeder Lauf
+   bekommt) dürfen zur Laufzeit gelesen werden. Die **Regeln** (Rechenlogik) dürfen wir implementieren.
+2. **Ein LLM entscheidet die Navigation**: wohin klicken, was suchen, welches Dokument relevant ist. Code darf helfen
+   (Seite extrahieren, ausgewähltes Dokument parsen, vom Modell gewählte Ergebnisliste paginieren, rechnen, validieren,
+   retry, Formular füllen). **Verboten**: fester Klickpfad, Crawler der alles einsammelt und am Ende einem Modell gibt.
+3. Keine eigenen Browser in der Sandbox starten (nur `CDP_URLS`), keine lokalen Modelle, kein Netzwerk außer
+   Plattform/Websites/Proxy, alle LLM-Calls über den Proxy (`*_BASE_URL`-Variablen).
+4. Keine Secrets im Repo. Eigene API-Keys nur als Team-Secret auf der Plattform.
+5. Nichts im Package, was den AI-Reviewer „steuern“ soll (Kommentare an den Reviewer zählen gegen uns).
+6. `submit`/`cancel` auf der Plattform **nur nach ausdrücklicher Freigabe eines Menschen**. Test-Runs sind frei.
+agent/                 # == eingereichtes Package (agent.json liegt HIER). Nur generischer Code!
+    contract.py        # Run laden (API / CHALLENGE_SCOUTING), Deadline, Logging
+    browser/           # session.py observe.py observe.js actions.py guards.py documents.py
+dev/                   # NICHT eingereicht: Scout-Tools, HTML-Fixtures der Public-Sites, Oracle, Eval-Harness
+Einreichen/Testen immer aus `agent/`: `atira test-run ./agent` (CLI packt den Ordner ohne `.gitignore`-Dateien).
+Alles mit Public-Werten (Fixtures, Oracle, Golden Answers) liegt ausschließlich in `dev/`.
+Brief ──► TaskContext (LLM-Extraktion: Referenz, Stichtag, Firma, USt-Id, Direktor-Mailbox, autorisierte Absender)
+     ├─ Explorer-Agent × 4  (je 1 Browser, LLM-Tool-Loop, Missionen = Informationsbedarf, NICHT Site-Skripte)
+     │     Tools: observe · click · fill · select · check · set_range · expand · goto_link · back · read_document
+     ├─ Blackboard: typisierte Facts mit Provenienz (Quelle, Datum, Referenz, Absender, Rohtext)
+     ├─ Resolver + Pricing (reines Python, Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP) ─► Answer-JSON + Rechenweg-Trace
+     └─ Submit-Agent: Konfigurator ausfüllen (LLM wählt Felder, Code verifiziert jeden Schritt),
+                      TAN anfordern → neueste TAN aus Mail → confirm()-Dialog akzeptieren
+- **LLM navigiert und interpretiert, Python rechnet.** Keine Arithmetik im LLM.
+- **Observation = eigener DOM-Serializer** (a11y-basiert, alle Frames, Tooltips + geschlossene `<details>` sichtbar,
+  Screenshots nur als Fallback für Vision (Qwen ist multimodal).
+- **Jede Zahl hat Provenienz** (Quelle + Rohtext + Locale). Resolver wendet „neuester datierter Eintrag ≤ Stichtag,
+  exakte Referenz, autorisierter Absender“ deterministisch an.
+- **Immer eine Antwort abgeben.** Deadline-Wächter: spätestens bei `expires_at − 4 min` mit bestem Stand signieren.
+  Leere Felder = 0 Punkte, falsche Felder = 0 Punkte → immer beste Schätzung eintragen, Positionen nie auslassen,
+  außer sie lassen sich technisch nicht konfigurieren.
+| `feat/browser-tools` | Browser-Robustheit | `browser/*` (Serializer, Actions, Guards, Documents), Fixture-Tests gegen `dev/fixtures` |
+| `feat/tender-specification` | Vergabe + Spezifikation | Missionen + Fact-Schemas für Tender, LV, Bieterfragen, Spezifikation/Revisionen, Nachträge |
+| `feat/erp-mail-evidence` | ERP + Mail | Missionen + Fact-Schemas für Material/Bestand/Konditionen, Mail-Freigaben, Keys |
+| `feat/pricing-submission` | Rechnen + Abgabe | `rules/*` (Parser, Resolver, Pricing, Validate), `submit/*` (Konfigurator, TAN) |
+Schnittstellen sind in `agent/rfq/facts.py` definiert (Owner: pricing-submission, Änderungen per PR mit Review
+durch orchestrator). Merge-Reihenfolge: orchestrator (Layout) → browser-tools → facts.py → Rest.
+- Python 3.12, `uv`, asyncio, Playwright (async), `pydantic` v2, `openai` SDK (für Qwen, OpenAI-kompatibel).
+  Keine weiteren schweren Abhängigkeiten ohne Absprache (Setup max. 5 min, Package ≤ 20 MB).

- **Everything in the browser:** your dashboard (`$API/team`) takes package uploads by drag and drop, lists every
  run with a link to its live view, and keeps your team's secrets.
- **Challenges:** each challenge is its own world with its own websites, task and answer format. The first one
  is [RFQ](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): turn a tender scattered across four German business websites into
  one priced bid.
- **Public and private data:** the websites and the scenario you scout and test-run on are the public dataset, and
  every scored submission runs on it during the hackathon. The correct answer isn't published; your system has to
  work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that
  passed review once by default, or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts, on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the winners
  ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from
  the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
- **Develop locally:** the scouting logins the organizers publish open the public websites to you and your agent.
  `atira scout --env` exports them the way a run gets its logins, so your agent runs on your machine against the
  real websites. Where the platform hosts models, they need no key there either: keep `atira models proxy` running
  and `--env` points your agent at it; any other provider takes your own key. Nothing done with them counts. RFQ has one public
  scenario, `public-1`.
- **Sandbox test runs:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live. It
  runs once in exactly the sandbox scored runs use, against the public scenario: watch its browser, read its logs,
  replay the recorded video, and get your score with the full breakdown. Use it to make sure your package works
  before you submit; `atira cancel` stops a run early.
- **Scored runs:** upload your agent system as a package. We review it, then run it once in the sandbox on the
  public dataset and score it. Only these runs count for the leaderboard. Your best submission holds your place on
  the leaderboard; your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
- **What wins:** eligible answers rank first, then answer quality; at equal quality, the lower LLM cost × wall-clock
  time wins, each measured on the submission's scored run. The final run ranks the same way, choosing your single best attempt if you opted in to three. Each public submission runs
  once.

##### building-an-agent
# Building your agent

Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
websites and hands everything to the model at the end.

## The browser

In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
`127.0.0.1:9222`.

- **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
- **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
  ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.

### Several browsers

To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:

```json
{"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
```

Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:

```javascript
import { chromium } from "playwright"

const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
```

At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.

## Models

The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
[how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
up.

## What makes it hard, on purpose

The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
every page as adversarial and verify what you read.

## Tips

- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.

## Starter kit

[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.
##### fair-play
# Fair play

**Rules at a glance**

You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.

**Not allowed**

- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.

**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.

The details follow.

## Allowed

- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
  amount of tokens.
  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
  for SDK configuration.
- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
  contexts inside them as you like.

## Not allowed

- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
  rules you may use.
- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.

## How it is checked

- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
  organizers' reason.
- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.

Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
get the team disqualified.

## Flagged results

A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
lists flagged results, without a rank.
##### scoring
# Answers and scoring

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).

## Per run

- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.

A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.

## Leaderboard

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
the run's own value.

1. Eligible before ineligible.
2. Higher quality.
3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.

On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
the teams no other eligible team beats on both.

Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.

## Final run

When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.

## Winners

We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:

1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
3. The elegance of the system.

It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).

## RFQ scoring

The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.

| Part (a bid) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | 5 |
| Tender reference | 5 |
| Discount percent | 5 |
| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |


For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
points but leaves the other fields their credit.

Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
one position's share each.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.

Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.
##### submitting
# Submitting

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.

## Package layout

```
agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
agent.py            your code
```

- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.

## Upload

```
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
```

The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.

`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).

Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.

## Test it in the sandbox first

Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
your team. Up to 4 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
test-run slot at once.

## Linking your GitHub repository

The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.

The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
settings.

## Watching your submission

Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
masked as `[private]`.

## Resubmitting

Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the

67	
68	Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes

76

83	- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
84	  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.

100	const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
101	const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))

119	## What makes it hard, on purpose
120	
121	The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
122	that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
123	"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat

126	## Tips
127	
128	- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
129	- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
130	- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
131	- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
132	- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
133	  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
134	- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
135	- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
136	  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
137	  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
138	- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
139	  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
140	- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
141	
142	## Starter kit
143	
144	[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
145	submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
146	Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.
147	##### fair-play
148	# Fair play
149	
150	**Rules at a glance**
151	
152	You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.
153	
154	**Not allowed**
155	
156	- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
157	- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
158	- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
159	- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.
160	
161	**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.
162	
163	The details follow.
164	
165	## Allowed
166	
167	- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
168	  amount of tokens.
169	  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
170	  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
171	  for SDK configuration.
172	- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
173	- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
174	- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
175	- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
176	  contexts inside them as you like.
177	
178	## Not allowed
179	
180	- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
181	  rules you may use.
182	- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
183	  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
184	  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
185	  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
186	  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
187	- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
188	- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
189	- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
190	  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
191	  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
192	- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.
193	
194	## How it is checked
195	
196	- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
197	  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
198	  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
199	  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
200	  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
201	  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
202	  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
203	  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
204	- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
205	  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
206	  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
207	  organizers' reason.
208	- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
209	- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
210	  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
211	  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
212	  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
213	  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
214	- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
215	  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
216	- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
217	- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
218	  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
219	- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.
220	
221	Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
222	get the team disqualified.
223	
224	## Flagged results
225	
226	A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
227	lists flagged results, without a rank.
228	##### scoring
229	# Answers and scoring
230	
231	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
232	
233	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
234	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
235	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
236	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
237	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
238	
239	## Per run
240	
241	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
242	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
243	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
244	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
245	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
246	
247	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
248	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
249	
250	## Leaderboard
251	
252	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
253	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
254	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
255	the run's own value.
256	
257	1. Eligible before ineligible.
258	2. Higher quality.
259	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
260	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
261	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
262	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
263	
264	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
265	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
266	
267	Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
268	values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
269	
270	## Final run
271	
272	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
273	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
274	
275	## Winners
276	
277	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
278	
279	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
280	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
281	3. The elegance of the system.
282	
283	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
284	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
285	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
286	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
287	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
288	
289	## RFQ scoring
290	
291	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
292	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
293	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
294	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
295	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
296	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
297	
298	| Part (a bid) | Points |
299	| --- | --- |
300	| Decision | 5 |
301	| Tender reference | 5 |
302	| Discount percent | 5 |
303	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
304	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
305	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
306	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
307	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
308	
309	
310	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
311	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
312	
313	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
314	one position's share each.
315	
316	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
317	
318	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
319	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
320	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
321	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
322	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
323	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
324	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
325	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
326	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
327	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
328	
329	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
330	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
331	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.
332	##### submitting
333	# Submitting
334	
335	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
336	
337	You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
338	and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
339	passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.
340	
341	## Package layout
342	
343	```
344	agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
345	pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
346	agent.py            your code
347	```
348	
349	- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
350	  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
351	  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
352	  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
353	  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
354	- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
355	- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.
356	
357	## Upload
358	
359	```
360	tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
361	curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
362	  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
363	  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
364	```
365	
366	The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
367	`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.
368	
369	`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
370	`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).
371	
372	Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
373	test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
374	your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.
375	
376	## Test it in the sandbox first
377	
378	Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
379	`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
380	the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
381	browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
382	and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
383	your team. Up to 4 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
384	and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
385	test-run slot at once.
386	
387	## Linking your GitHub repository
388	
389	The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
390	code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
391	Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
392	(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
393	who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.
394	
395	The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
396	settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
397	described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
398	settings.
399	
400	## Watching your submission
401	
402	Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
403	shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
404	unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
405	screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
406	masked as `[private]`.
407	
408	## Resubmitting
409	
410	Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the
411	next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
412	**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
413	`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you
414	can submit again.
415	
416	## What happens next
417	
418	1. **Review:** passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged submission still runs and scores, but its result
419	   stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it marked
420	   "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Your team sees the outcome, not the reviewer's reasons. The organizers can
421	   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
422	   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.
423	2. **Scored run:** one run in a fresh sandbox on the public dataset, setup first (up to 5 minutes, not counted),
424	   then your run command (timed).
425	3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
426	   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.
427	4. **Final run:** when the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review
428	   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. It is the latest one, not the best one.
429	   That run weighs most when we pick the winners ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to
430	   the public scenario. Its results stay with the organizers until they publish them; then the leaderboard shows
431	   the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", and the public-dataset board stays at
432	   `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.
433	
434	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
435	
436	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team

It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
485	That run weighs most when we pick the winners, ahead of your public score and the elegance of your system, so

503	
504	**Why do my requests get a 403 "Error 1010"?** The edge in front of our hosts refuses some default HTTP
505	clients, such as Python's `urllib`. Send your own `User-Agent` header (the starter kit does).
506	
507	**Python says `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on my Mac.** Python from python.org ships without CA certificates.
508	Run `Install Certificates.command` from its folder in Applications, or set `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem`.
509	
510	**What can my agent reach during a scored run?** Our API (including the model proxy) and the challenge's
511	websites, nothing else. The `HTTP(S)_PROXY` variables in the run's environment route there; Python's
512	`urllib`, `requests`, `httpx`, the Anthropic SDK and Node's `fetch` pick them up automatically. Chromium is
513	already configured. Setup (`uv sync`, `npm ci`, …) has network, but nothing it starts survives into the
514	run.
515	
516	## Event details
517	
518	- The event is on 10 October 2026.
519	- A team has up to five people.
520	- A scored run has 20 minutes on the clock; a test run has up to 2 hours.
521	- Ask the organizers about the submission deadline and prizes.
522	
523	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
524	
525	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
526	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
527	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).
528	##### demo-day
529	# Demo day
530	
531	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
532	
533	The best teams run their agent live on stage against the public scenario while the room watches the live run
534	view.
535	
536	- **The live run view** at `$API/runs/<run id>` shows the team, a running timer, LLM calls and tokens per model,
537	  the cost so far, and the score once the answer is in. Its timer ticks every second and the rest refreshes every
538	  two seconds; it is what the projector shows.
539	- **Your agent's screen:** run it on your laptop with a visible browser, or in our sandbox, whose desktop we can
540	  show.
541	- **Prepare:** a one-line command that starts your agent, such as `atira test-run ./my-agent` (it opens the run
542	  page), a reliable network, and a fallback recording.
